etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English upholden, equivalent to up- +‎ hold. Compare Dutch ophouden (“to stop, cease, hold up”), German aufhalten (“to stop, halt, detain”). Compare also Middle Low German upholt, Old Norse upphald (“uphold, support”).

definitions.definition: To hold up; to lift on high; to elevate.

quote.citation: 1899, John Dryden, Geoffrey Chaucer, Percival Chubb, Dryden's Palamon and Arcite‎[1], page 5:
quote.text: The mournful train/ Echoed her grief, [...]/ With groans, and hands upheld, to move his mind, /Besought his pity to their helpless kind

definitions.definition: To keep erect; to support; to sustain; to keep from falling

quote.text: A man's pride shall bring him low: but honour shall uphold the humble in spirit.

quote.citation: 1623, William Shakespeare, The Life and Death of King John, Act V, Scene iv:
quote.text: That misbegotten devil, Falconbridge, /In spite of spite, alone upholds the day.

quote.citation: 1872, James De Mille, The Cryptogram‎[2], HTML edition, The Gutenberg Project, published 2009:
quote.text: Uttering such broken ejaculations Mrs. Hart burst into a passion of tears, and only Lord Chetwynde's strong arms prevented her from falling. / He upheld her.

quote.citation: Wednesday June 02, 2021, Has the Northern Ireland Protocol undermined the United Kingdom?
quote.text: Similarly, both the Government and the EU argued at the time the deal was agreed that they were upholding the Good Friday Agreement by implementing the Protocol.

definitions.definition: To support by approval or encouragement; to vindicate; to confirm (something which has been questioned)

quote.citation: 1748, David Hume, Enquiries concerning the human understanding and concerning the principles of moral., London: Oxford University Press, published 1973, § 18:
quote.text: but there was still a connexion upheld among the different ideas, which succeeded each other.
